A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConG study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen and Llama alignment experiments, downstream evaluations, coefficient and model-capacity analyses, cross-family results, and generated-response case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds comparator results, training-time measurements, and evaluations using GPT-5 and human judges.

M1.justification: Both versions generate chosen responses through contrastive decoding between pre- and post-alignment weak models, train the strong model with SFT, and apply DPO using responses sampled from that SFT model as rejected examples. Algorithm 1 and the objectives are unchanged; removing the repeated weak-model decoding equation does not change the procedure.

E1.justification: Both use UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval2, Arena-Hard, and the same downstream benchmarks, including ARC, TruthfulQA, MMLU, MathQA, HellaSwag, and GSM8K. Cross-family alignment already appears in v1. The new judging and timing experiments do not introduce new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Weak SFT (post) and WeakTeacher to the central strong-model comparisons. The original Weak SFT results are retained as Weak SFT (pre). These additions substantially strengthen the comparison by including an aligned-teacher control and a competitive additional method; Tables 2 and 3 retain their original comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix D.3 adds GPT-5 judging and a protocol labeled '10% Human Evaluation' alongside the retained GPT-4 evaluations, substantially extending how alignment quality is assessed. Appendix D.2 also introduces GPU-hour measurement. Existing training settings and benchmark metrics remain unchanged; the human sampling and rating procedures are insufficiently specified.

E4.justification: New Appendices D.2-D.3 investigate computational cost and dependence on the evaluator, supported by Tables 4-6. These add substantial efficiency and judge-robustness analyses beyond the retained coefficient, model-capacity, response-length, cross-family, and case-study analyses.

E5.justification: The retained tables preserve their uncertainty entries, Table 3 still specifies mean and standard deviation, and Figure 3 retains standard-error bars. No run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are newly disclosed. The new timing and judging tables provide point estimates without additional uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: All matched numerical rows in Tables 1-3 remain unchanged, but v2 adds two comparator rows and the timing and judging results in Tables 4-6. For example, WeakTeacher averages 43.5/32.6 for Qwen/Llama, below ConG's retained 52.7/41.6. ConG's new GPT-5 averages of 47.3/36.6 and human-evaluation averages of 55.2/44.1 concern different judging conditions, not performance changes from v1.

T1.justification: Section 3 and the supplementary proofs, moved from Appendix D to C, retain the same mathematical reasoning and reward-ordering assertions. 'Equivalence' becomes 'Correlation,' but the actual derivations are unchanged. Refactoring Equation 7 and removing a repeated decoding equation are presentational changes.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims about contrastive decoding, implicit-reward maximization, capability transfer, denoising, and robustness. Although the named connection changes from 'Equivalence' to 'Correlation,' the abstract still asserts structural equivalence and the substantive maximization claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations attributing comparable optimization costs to offline data construction and consistent performance to robustness across judges. Appendix B.2 newly explains WSPO's reduced performance through its restriction to self-generated responses. The Impact Statement adds possible low-resource applications and residual propagation of weak-model biases; Section 7's limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 reports training times on the already specified four L40 GPUs and expands documentation of WSPO's self-generated-data adaptation, which v1 already described more briefly. Original hyperparameters and the code link remain. The dedicated reproducibility statement specifying released configurations and evaluation scripts is removed, without establishing that those resources were withdrawn.

R1.justification: Section 6 replaces the Ji and Shen survey citations with Cao and Gao surveys and adds references concerning WeakTeacher, safety interventions, multimodal reasoning, and on-policy distillation. These broaden the discussion modestly while preserving the central positioning around connecting weak-to-strong generalization with implicit rewards and contrastive decoding.

P1.justification: Most exposition and section order are retained. Targeted edits rename the CD connection, expand selected explanations, replace the ethics/reproducibility end matter with impact and acknowledgment statements, remove the LLM-usage appendix, and revise author affiliations. Editorial errors include an unrelated running title and a broken sentence in Section 5.1.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column ICLR layout to a two-column ICML layout, substantially resizing and repositioning figures, tables, and equations. Table 1 gains rows and Tables 4-6 are added. Figure 1's connection label changes, while Figures 2-3 retain their original graphics.

improvement.justification: Adding post-alignment Weak SFT and WeakTeacher makes the central comparison more informative: both improve on the base models, yet ConG remains ahead. Alternative-judge results and training-time reporting provide useful additional support. The gain is limited by the underspecified human evaluation, missing offline-generation cost accounting, and editorial errors, including the unrelated running header.
